titleEn: In God I trust, I will not be afraid
progression: | Dm Dm | Gm Dm | Bb C | Dm Dm |
intro: Fourteen verses of pressure, and the heading pins them to the worst moment of David's flight: seized by the Philistines in Gath, the city of the champion he had killed, where the book of Samuel has him feign madness to get out alive. The psalm answers that pressure with a refrain rather than an argument, saying the same sentence at verse 5 and again at verse 12 with one word changed. For a learner it is a drill in suffixes: nearly every verb of attack in the first half ends in -ni, me, and nearly every noun of comfort in the second half ends in -kha, Yours.

stichs.en: For the leader, on the tune of the silent dove of distant places.
Of David. A michtam.
When the Philistines seized him in Gath.

verses.summary: The heading gives a tune name nobody can now identify and a setting anyone can. Gath is enemy ground, and the psalm that follows is spoken from inside it.

stichs.en: Be gracious to me, God,
for a mortal snaps at me;
all day long a fighter presses me hard.

verses.summary: The first word is the request and the whole psalm compressed. What follows is the reason, and the reason is a man: enosh, a mortal, is doing this.

stichs.en: My watchers snap at me all day long,
for many fight against me, O Most High.

verses.summary: The verb of verse 2 comes back in the plural. One attacker becomes many, and the last word of the line is read either as an address to God or as a description of how the enemies fight.

stichs.en: The day I am afraid,
I put my trust in You.

verses.summary: Three words of fear and two of trust, with the trust placed second. The psalm never claims the fear is unfounded, only that it is not the last move.

stichs.en: In God, whose word I praise,
in God I trust, I will not be afraid.
What can flesh do to me?

verses.summary: The refrain. Trust is stated in the perfect tense, as something already done, and the closing question is not open: flesh is exactly what the enemy is made of.

stichs.en: All day long they twist my words against me;
all their thoughts are for harm.

verses.summary: The attack moves from the body to speech. They take his words and bend them, which is what happens to anyone whose enemy controls the account of him.

stichs.en: They band together, they lie hidden;
they themselves watch my heels,
just as they have waited for my life.

verses.summary: Four verbs of surveillance in a row. The enemy here is patient rather than violent: gathering, hiding, tracking the heels, waiting.

stichs.en: For such iniquity, is there escape for them?
In anger bring the peoples down, God.

verses.summary: The one verse that turns aggressive, and also the one whose Hebrew is hardest to construe. What is asked is that the same measure fall back on the attackers.

stichs.en: My wandering You Yourself have counted;
put my tears in Your flask.
Are they not in Your record?

verses.summary: The image the psalm is remembered for. Tears are not spilled and lost, they are collected and filed, and the wandering itself has already been counted.

stichs.en: Then my enemies will turn back on the day I call.
This I know: that God is for me.

verses.summary: The turn. Everything before this was request, and from here it is knowledge. Note what does the turning: not a battle, but the calling itself.

stichs.en: In God, whose word I praise,
in the LORD, whose word I praise.

verses.summary: The refrain returns, and this time the same line is said twice, once with each divine name. Nothing else in the verse changes.

stichs.en: In God I trust, I will not be afraid.
What can a human being do to me?

verses.summary: Verse 5 said again with one word changed: flesh becomes adam. The threat has now been named twice and cut down to size twice.

stichs.en: Upon me, God, are the vows I owe You;
I will pay thank offerings to You.

verses.summary: Vows made under pressure now come due. Thanks here is not a feeling but an obligation with a weight, something owed and brought.

stichs.en: For You have rescued my life from death,
have You not kept my feet from stumbling,
so that I may walk before God in the light of the living?

verses.summary: The reason for the vow, stated in the perfect tense as already done. Rescue from death is only half of it; the other half is a foot that does not slip, and the point of both is walking.

pardes.body: The shape is complaint, refrain, complaint, refrain, vow. Verses 2 and 3 describe the attack, 4 and 5 answer it, 6 to 8 describe it again from a different angle, and 9 to 12 answer it again and harder. The refrain is the load-bearing structure: verse 5 and verse 12 are the same sentence with one substitution, {{5.9}} becoming {{12.6}}, flesh becoming a human being. Both words mean the same thing here, that the enemy is mortal, and saying it twice is the argument. The vow at verse 13 belongs to the same logic: a person who has decided the rescue is real starts owing thanks for it before it arrives.

Verse 9 turns on sound. {{9.0}}, my wandering, and {{9.5}}, Your flask, are near-identical noises from unrelated roots, and the line puts them one after the other so that the wandering and the container for what the wandering produced rhyme. Two other places are genuinely unsettled. {{3.8}} can be a vocative, O Most High, or an adverb describing how the enemies fight, arrogantly, and translations split on it. {{8.2}} is harder still: read as a noun the line asks whether such people get to escape, read as an imperative it asks God to cast them out, and the difference is one of vocalization rather than consonants.

The tune name of the superscription, the silent dove of distant places, has long been read in the tradition as a description rather than a melody: Israel far from home and unable to speak for itself, which turns a psalm about one man surrounded in Gath into a psalm the community can say. The setting supports the reading, since the David of 1 Samuel 21 survives Gath precisely by making himself unintelligible, scratching at the gates and letting spit run down his beard. The counted wandering of verse 9 is then read as exile counted rather than one flight, and the tears kept in a flask as the claim that nothing of it is lost.

Verse 11 praises the same word twice, once under the name Elohim and once under the four-letter Name, and the standard reading of that pair takes the first as judgement and the second as mercy. The verse then says that the promise is worth praising whichever way it arrives, which is a harder claim than gratitude for rescue and is made before any rescue has happened. The flask and the record of verse 9 are two images of the same thing, a memory that keeps what the world discards, and in the mystical reading tears are not evidence of weakness but a measure being filled, which is why the psalm can ask for them to be stored rather than stopped.
